items.text:
Artist Sally J. Han is an exacting painter with a meticulous eye. Her detailed, colorful works depict some of life’s most ordinary moments—scrolling on a phone, peeling fruit—yet are juxtaposed with surrealist elements. Han often does this through scale. In Satellite of Love , for instance, a diminutive figure wearing a hanbok sits on a rock gazing up at an impossibly large moon that takes over the composition. It’s something we’d imagine many of us doing; however, in Han’s hands, it takes on a fantastical feel that invites many interpretations.
Han has a multicultural background, and art has served as a bridge between cultures. “From an early age, I thought of drawing as a form of communication,” she tells My Modern Met. “Having grown up in South Korea and China, and later moving to the U.S., I sometimes relied on simple sketches to express myself when I wasn’t yet familiar with the language of each country. I had always enjoyed drawing as a child, but living in different countries made it feel less like a talent and more like my own familiar way of expressing myself.”
We follow the same figure throughout Han’s work. Like the artist, the figure exists in different landscapes, including a desert sunset, a verdant tropical garden, and on a large porch with a yard. Carefully rendered elements dot the composition, like animals, tipped-over soda cans, and a pair of eyeglasses held loosely in a hand. Individually, the common objects aren’t anything special. But in Han’s visual language, they become layered and lyrical, touching on ideas of tradition and our own mythology, and ultimately shaped by our own analysis.
“I find that the familiarity and comfort of everyday life can often feel surprisingly new when viewed from a different perspective,” she explains. “I think what I enjoy most is discovering those moments.” Cultures different from her own have always fascinated her. “But what I find even more interesting is the sense of connection we can share despite our differences. I’ve always been drawn to the human side of things, and I think that naturally finds its way into my paintings.”
Han recently concluded a solo exhibition titled Gazing at Lee Art Consulting in Seoul. She’s currently working on paintings that will debut in spring 2027 at Dan Yoshii in New York City.

items.text:
A married couple is spending their time cleaning filthy street signs—with dreams of traveling across the country until they are all spotless.
Paul and Ruth Richmond-Watson started scrubbing street signs in September after feeling the urge to find a new hobby they could do together.
“We are both autistic with ADHD, so we are quite creative and a bit weird,” explained Paul, who is a former window washer himself. “We just thought we could really make this work.”
The duo in Brighton, England, had noticed that a lot of their local traffic signage was unreadable at night due to the grime, so they got to work clearing it themselves.
The couple are now cleaning at least one sign a day, taking videos to post on social media.
Although they’re only cleaning locally in East Sussex at the moment, Paul says they have dreams of road tripping across the UK to cover more ground.
Originally from New Zealand, the 47-year-old said the couple is “very community focused”.
“Neighbors just don’t ‘neighbor’ anymore, and we wanted to do something that would help out.
“It was for our mental health as well, to get out-and-about and have a reason to leave the house.
“Britain is quite unique in having filthy road signs. It is a bit of a state really, and we are just trying to smarten it up.”
The newlyweds fund their own efforts, but also gained a couple sponsorships—with supply companies.
On average, it takes around 20-25 minutes for each sign, using a backpack water pump with a hose, a snow foam gun with environmentally-friendly foam, and a long-handled brush.
25-year-old Ruth said, “A lot of dirty signs are hard to read, especially at night. We notice patterns, so we were always commenting on it when we were driving around.”
“The first one that we did, it was a bit of a learning curve but, it was so satisfying and fun. It is quite a bonding experience for us.”
Since posting on their Instagram account @Filthy_signs, the pair have received lots of supportive comments, and are being recognized by other locals.
“Driving past it a few weeks later and seeing it still sparkle is amazing,” said Paul. “You feel quite proud of yourself.
“Everyone is really behind us. It has been incredible. It is overwhelming in a good way. We didn’t expect it to blow up like this, and are just literally having fun.”

Curated by Ana Carolina Ralston, the exhibition examines how urban development reshapes collective memory and individual identity. VHILS uses acid, oxidation, and subtraction to transform corroded metal into layered compositions. The works bring together visual traces of Lisbon, São Paulo, and Shanghai. A large-scale intervention on the gallery’s glass facade also extends the exhibition into the surrounding city.
Since beginning his career in graffiti in the early 2000s, VHILS has expanded his practice to include bas-relief carving, metal etching, wood carving, sculpture, and site-specific installations. His work considers what is lost as cities change, particularly as globalization and development threaten established communities. After more than a decade of working with Brazilian communities, he returns to São Paulo with these questions at the center of his latest exhibition.
Atrito: Arqueologia do Presente opens on November 14 and runs through February 20, 2027 at Galleria Continua São Paulo.

items.title: How many sewage spills have happened in your part of Scotland?
items.desc: More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded at overflow sites previously unmonitored by Scottish Water, BBC Scotland News analysis has found.
items.text:
More than 76,000 sewage spills were recorded after new monitoring equipment was installed at waste overflow sites in Scotland, BBC analysis suggests.
The addition of 1,009 sewer monitors in 2024 increased the proportion of the Scottish Water network being monitored from 6% to 30%.
Now the latest figures have revealed tens of thousands of spills which would previously have been unrecorded, including hundreds at beauty spots like Loch Lomond.
Scottish Water said the vast majority of the spills were not harmful to the environment, and that increased monitoring had improved understanding of the sewer network.
BBC Scotland News has used the latest data to create an interactive map which you can use to find out how many spills were recorded in your area, and how long they lasted.
Sewage spills happen automatically at overflow sites, which are permitted to release excess water into natural waterways.
They usually consist of a pipe - set much higher than the usual water level - which provides an escape route when the system is deluged.
These overflows act as relief valves to prevent the sewer system from becoming overwhelmed during heavy rainfall and flooding into homes, businesses and streets.
The spills can last anywhere from a few minutes to hours.
Scottish Water currently has over 4,200 overflows across its network. The number of overflows with monitoring rose from 273 to 1,275 in 2024.
More than 100,000 spills totalling to almost 277,000 hours were recorded last year – an average of about 274 a day.
It is difficult to assess how the numbers compare to the previous year's figures, when 24,000 spills were recorded because of lower coverage.
The sites are all licensed to release untreated or partially-treated waste but just under 12% of overflows are legally required to report their data to the regulator, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).
Sepa said it has a "risk-based approach" which prioritises areas for monitoring based on population and environmental need.
However, none of the new monitors were required to be reported to Sepa.

items.desc: A Catholic health care system in the American Midwest has successfully completed the world’s first reported bone marrow transplant to treat a non-malignant disease. items.text:
A Catholic health care system in the American Midwest has successfully completed the world’s first reported bone marrow transplant to treat a non-malignant disease.
Doctors at Franciscan Health used bone marrow recovered from a deceased organ donor to treat a 40-year-old woman with aplastic anemia
The patient, with a decade-long history of the disease, received the bone marrow stem cell transplant on April 18, after her disease progressed from stable to severe, despite multiple lines of therapy.
Because her disease no longer responded to medication, her care team pursued a transplant to replace her failing marrow with healthy blood-forming stem cells.
Six months after the transplant, the donor marrow has taken hold and restored her blood counts.
She no longer needs blood or platelet transfusions and has achieved full donor chimerism, meaning her blood and immune system are now produced entirely by the donor’s stem cells, without complications.
For non-malignant conditions including severe aplastic anemia, sickle cell disease, beta thalassemia, and other inherited or acquired bone marrow failure disorders, bone marrow-derived stem cells are widely regarded as the preferred stem cell source over peripheral blood stem cells (PBSCs), and the source of choice for non-malignant diseases.
“Bone marrow transplantation for severe aplastic anemia has been performed since the 1970s using living related and unrelated donors.
“To our knowledge, this is the first reported transplant of deceased organ donor bone marrow for severe aplastic anemia,” said Felix Mensah, MD, the treating physician at Franciscan Health.
“This case shows why continued innovation in transplant medicine matters, and why we need more donor options, so that every patient with a life-threatening bone marrow failure disorder has access to potentially curative therapy.”
“Reaching the first non-malignant transplant is a defining moment,” said Kevin Caldwell , Co-Founder and CEO of Ossium, which maintains a marrow bank.
“By recovering and banking bone marrow from organ donors, we can consistently optimize treatment outcomes.”

items.title: Bluetongue virus confirmed on County Down farm
items.desc: Officials from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs said the virus had been detected in three sheep.
items.text:
Spread by midges, bluetongue poses no threat to the public or food safety
The first case of Bluetongue in Northern Ireland this season has been confirmed on a farm in Kilkeel, County Down.
Officials from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) said the virus had been detected in three sheep.
There will be no additional movement restrictions or disease control zones, because the virus has been present in Northern Ireland since November 2025.
The minister, Andrew Muir, said the discovery of the virus was "disappointing but not unexpected", given the spread of the disease in Great Britain and Ireland.
The Chief Veterinary Officer, Brian Dooher, urged local farmers to be alert to any symptoms in their livestock.
The confirmation of the virus in Kilkeel comes after more than 100 cases across the Republic of Ireland in recent months.
Cases in England have been increasing, with 2,950 now confirmed.
There have been 512 cases in Wales and 57 in Scotland.
The mild winter means more of the biting midge that spreads the disease are likely to have survived and become infectious this season.
Muir said awareness was key, adding: "Continued vigilance and strict biosecurity measures remain of paramount importance and I would once again urge all farmers to report any suspicion of disease to Daera.
"It is important that I reiterate that Bluetongue poses no threat to public health nor to food safety – milk and meat are safe to consume."
Dooher said any suspected cases on farms should be reported to Daera.
"Active surveillance is ongoing at abattoirs alongside post-import testing of susceptible animals imported from mainland EU countries.
"I also want to stress the importance of safe and responsible sourcing of animals."
The disease was first detected in Northern Ireland near Bangor in County Down in November 2025.
A number of other herds along the eastern coast of Northern Ireland have also been affected.
Farmers have been urged to vaccinate their animals.
The disease affects ruminants such as cattle, sheep, goats and deer.

items.title: Burnham says climate consensus 'gone' but pledges 'new era of leadership'
items.desc: PM Andy Burnham was addressing delegates at the COP31 UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey.
items.text:
PM Andy Burnham was the only G7 leader to go to COP31
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has warned that the consensus on both science and climate change has "gone".
Addressing other world leaders and delegates at the COP31 climate summit in Turkey, he said that despite this, the UK was ready to begin a "new era of British leadership" on the climate change issue.
But environmental campaigners at the summit said the PM had to back up his warm words with stronger actions.
In recent months, the UK government has announced policies which critics say have weakened its green credentials, such as reducing support for heat pumps, approving the Jackdaw gas field and doubling down on support for Heathrow Airport's expansion.
Burnham opened his speech on Thursday by talking about the heat experienced in the UK this past summer.
He said "it was not normal" - in fact it was the hottest on record, made 130 times more likely because of climate change, according to the Met Office .
Hundreds of schools were closed, cereal harvests were down 11%, and ambulance services were inundated with calls beyond levels seen during the Covid-19 pandemic.
As a result of the threat to people's health and homes, the PM said he was creating the UK, and the world's, first climate security envoy, Dame Madeleine Alessandri.
Alessandri, the former head of the Joint Intelligence Committee, said: "Climate change and nature loss are increasingly shaping the security environment in which the UK operates."
As a result this was "placing additional pressure on resources, economies and communities around the world", she added.
This will be seen as a strong indication of the focus of the UK's priorities when it takes up the G20 presidency next year.
The current president is the US, which has been a notable absentee from the COP process over the last two years since President Trump withdrew the country from the most important global climate treaty - the Paris Climate Agreement.
Professor Lord Nicholas Stern, who identified 20 years ago that climate change could cost the global economy up to 20% of GDP if left unchecked, praised the PM's words.
"The Prime Minister was right to identify climate change as a threat to security around the world, and the importance of investments in clean electricity generation as the best way of protecting households and businesses from the high prices and volatile markets for fossil fuels," he said.

items.text:
The world’s largest demonstration plant for a new kind of renewable energy storage is up and running in the west of the China.
Called liquid-air energy storage (LAES) the plant uses renewable electricity to compress air to extreme densities until it turns to liquid. It can then be rapidly released to power a turbine and discharge that green energy back into the grid.
China has received numerous plaudits for its rapid adoption of renewable energy at both scale and speed, and this new facility in Qinghai Province brings in a key missing element to the renewable build-out: grid-scale battery storage for when the Sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing.
Not that either of those happen very often in Qinghai, which encompasses parts of the Tibetan Plateau, and Mongolia-like grasslands and desert, where both sun and wind are famously relentless.
Described as “the world’s largest grid-connected liquid-air energy storage facility by both rated power and energy capacity,” the facility is rated at 600 megawatt-hours, and will substantially back up the renewable contribution to the regional power grid by providing 10 hours of continual power supply when necessary. Additionally, it was built with its own solar farm, rated at 250MW.
LAES works by turning ordinary air into a liquid, keeping that liquid in insulated tanks, and then converting it back into electricity when needed.
When electricity is plentiful, it powers machinery that draws in air, compresses it and cools it to extremely low temperatures of around -190°C. At this point, the air becomes a liquid, taking up far less space than it did as a gas.
When power is needed, the liquid air is pumped to high pressure and warmed. As it warms, it rapidly expands back into a gas and can be used to spin a turbine connected to an electricity generator, sending power back to the grid.
A cool party trick is how the system utilizes the excess heat and cold: it stores both for heating and cooling the air as needed, reducing energy consumption and environmental disturbance.

items.text:
The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art has finally opened, after 17 years of work put into its creation by George Lucas and his wife, businesswoman Mellody Hobson. While it has drawn large crowds from all walks of life, its proud founders have not forgotten that for many, particularly students and low-income families, museum pricing can be high, resulting in some missing out on a lunch or a treat during a visit. As such, they’ve implemented a few measures to keep it budget-friendly for everyone.
The inspiration behind this lies in Hobson’s personal story. While today she is president and co-CEO of Ariel Investments, and a former chair of both DreamWorks and Starbucks, Hobson grew up in poverty. Her mother, a single parent of six, struggled to make ends meet, sometimes not even having enough money to pay the rent. As a result of this financial challenge, Hobson often found herself unable to afford any food as a kid on a field trip at a museum. These experiences marked her profoundly. In fact, it prompted the couple to create affordable options for all visitors to their museum, where the lobby café offers $2 grilled cheese sandwiches. These simply yet satisfying sandwiches are made with American and cheddar cheese melted together between slices of buttered Pullman bread.
“That was the directive from the founders, George and Mellody,” Katie Harel, the restaurant’s managing director, told Forbes , “who were adamant that there would be something affordable in the café for everyone. So everyone can eat something in the café for $2. Every single person.” In addition to the grilled cheese option, the museum café also offers a $3 peanut butter and jelly sandwich.
Since no museum visit is complete without a trip to the gift shop, the Lucas Museum also offers some affordable souvenirs. The on-site shop sells 25¢ pencils listed as the Mellody Pencil . Part of the First Draft Collection , the stylish pencils include cheeky markings indicating how much of the pencil it would take to write a first, second, third, and final draft. The museum also offers a large selection of postcards for $2 each.
To plan your visit and book tickets, check out the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art website. To stay up to date with the museum, you can follow the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art on Instagram .

items.text:
A penned draft of the famous ‘I have a Dream’ speech, written by Martin Luther King Jr. the morning of the famous event on the Lincoln Memorial, has resurfaced after 6 decades.
Unlike any other examples of his longhand writing ever found, the draft’s copious revisions tell of a man who understood the gravity of what he was preparing to say.
The New York Times reports that King’s own draft of the speech had been presumed lost. Those which are known had all been drafted and or typed up by his aides.
Now, Xernona Clayton, the widow of King’s former aide Edward Clayton, has revealed to the nation in its 250th year that she had found the handwritten draft in her deceased husband’s desk drawer in the 1990s, but only recently decided to put it up for auction at Christie’s for the benefit of several charities, including the King Center in Atlanta.
She found it one day in an envelope marked “Speech,” and though she recognized the words immediately, it never occurred to her that it might have been written by the speaker himself.
“This is the most important manuscript I’ve ever had the honor to handle,” Peter Klarnet, Christie’s manuscript specialist, told the Times, adding that he couldn’t imagine getting his hands on anything better that he “wouldn’t have to steal out of the National Archives.”
This relic of American oratory consists of 7 yellow pages covered in blue ink. Words, and sometimes whole paragraphs are crossed out. In some cases, a word was crossed out to be replaced by another word which was also crossed out.
It captures the mood in the Washington hotel where Dr. King was working on the speech with his colleagues who had spent days exploring various themes and directions it might take. He had been told to limit the speech to 5 minutes—pressure—all while knowing that President John Kennedy had only 2 months prior sent the proposed Civil Rights Act to Congress where it had not yet been voted on—more pressure.

The draft is very close to the typed document which King set before the microphones, yet it’s unclear whether the large crossed out sections—which have already undergone digital examination—will reveal new insights into King’s ideas, or mood at the time.
Just like the master copy, the draft doesn’t include the section that begins with “I have a dream” which King famously improvised. It does conclude with “Free at last.”

Named Fountain Plaza Tirana, the project won over designs presented by four other international firms. Conceived as a mixed-use building, Fountain Plaza Tirana will stand several feet above Rinia Park, preserving and expanding the public park area while making room for a new hotel, apartments, offices, and cultural spaces.
The building evokes a dense cloud formation above the park. To achieve this, layers of rounded, perforated white terraces rest on slim columns, while two wider structures at opposite ends of the building house the elevators that provide floor access. To avoid breaking with the “floating” concept, these elements are clad in flute glass to let light shine through and onto the park.

Ada Le Poidevin was living on the island of Guernsey in the English Channel when she sheltered three British soldiers left behind during a raid on the Nazi-occupied land in 1940.

Ada and her husband Walter offered their garden shed for them to hide in, despite severe consequences if the trio were to be discovered.
All three survived the conflict and they remained close to Ada and Walter, regularly returning to Guernsey to visit them and even attending the couple’s Golden Wedding celebration.
It was the second time Ada had put herself in danger during wartime. During WWI, she spent two years supporting British troops in France working in camps that came under enemy fire—and suffered heavy damage.

After 100 years, Gretchen Sollo had a major first: a surprise birthday party, thrown by the Lowe’s employees she sees every day.
Following a stroke, Sollo turned to the aisles of Lowe’s for her daily walk and to keep out of the weather in Bradley, Illinois. She’s since walked an estimated 1,500 miles over five years, creating a daily ritual and friendships with staff members that stretched around the store.
Store associates check on her number of laps and even challenge her to races, joining her on her walks around the store. If there’s ever a day Sollo doesn’t show up, staff members notice and worry.
Store manager Joe Jackson gave her the honorary title of “store mom.”
Once Jackson and staff found out Sollo was turning 100 on November 1, 2026, they knew they had to do something special.
When Sollo showed up for her daily laps on October 30, she was joined by Jackson. Jackson guided Sollo over to a decorated aisle where a blue carpet led to an arch of birthday balloons, a cake and a personalized Lowe’s vest for Sollo. The aisle was lined by around 50 associates (some who came on their day off), friends, family and Sollo’s son Hugh.
“I never wanted a birthday party,” Sollo told People in an exclusive interview, adding “Means I missed out on a lot, I guess.”
A woman who spent a century working, raising a family, and staying active finally took a moment to allow others to show how much they cared – they just had to meet her where she already was.

“I have only worked one Friday 13th wedding in my 14 years in business,” says Caroline Smyth, a photographer and celebrant based in Larne, Northern Ireland. “I definitely think it is down to the fact that it’s a date surrounded by superstition. People are maybe afraid it’s a bad omen for their marriage.”
Smyth’s sole Friday 13th wedding, in September 2013, was the first she ever photographed – and it kickstarted her career. But for many businesses, the date is not so auspicious. From weddings to flights, job interviews to elective surgeries, many people avoid booking anything of significance on this date, believing it to be bad luck.
Today is the third Friday 13th in 2026 – the maximum number of times this date can occur in any year in the Gregorian calendar, and the only such year this decade. The last year with three Friday 13ths was 2015. But where does western wariness of this date come from – and is there any evidence that it does bring bad luck?
The origins of the superstition are not entirely clear. Some believe the number 13 to be unlucky in itself, thanks to a mix of religious, folkloric and cultural traditions. items.desc: El Niño winters typically bring more rain in the southern USA and drier, warmer conditions further north but the impacts on snowfall are complex.
items.text:
Montreal, Canada was badly hit by the Great Ice Storm of 1998 which was blamed, in part, on El Niño.
The developing El Niño - already the strongest on record by some measures - continues to grow and could have profound effects on the weather across North America this autumn and winter.
The naturally-occurring climate phenomenon sees trade winds over the Pacific Ocean, which usually blow from east to west, weakening or reversing with warm water instead spreading eastwards.
This releases heat into the atmosphere which can drive major shifts in global weather patterns.
Impacts in the US and Canada are varied, with a greater chance of a warm and dry winter in northern areas and more risk of flooding rain further south.
There is also some evidence that El Niño can increase the likelihood of disruption to the stratospheric polar vortex which can, in turn, bring snowfall later in winter.
No two El Niños are the same and the impacts are not guaranteed - the odds are just shifted in favour of certain outcomes.
UN warns of 'supersized' El Niño as countries prepare for impact
The eastward shift of warm ocean waters associated with El Niño can cause the Pacific jet stream to move south and extend eastwards, directing rain-bearing weather systems across the southern USA.
This typically leads to wetter winters during El Niño years.
The likely impacts of El Niño on winter weather vary across different parts of North America.
The latest three month forecast , external from the US National Weather Service (NWS) suggests this is a likely outcome for the winter of 2026-2027.
South-eastern states, including Florida, Georgia and the Carolinas, have the greatest chance of seeing above-average rainfall.
The El Niño winter of 1997-1998 brought significant flooding in the south-east and spun up tornadoes for Florida.
Severe flooding hit Long Beach, California in February 2024.
California could well find itself in the firing line with forecasts suggesting a wet winter is likely.
Governor Gavin Newsom has already declared a state of emergency , external ahead of anticipated floods and mudslides.
Areas scarred by recent wildfires are particularly susceptible, with the effects of climate change exacerbating the risks.
Many past El Niños have been wet here, with winter 2023-2024 bringing relief from drought. However this is not always the case. In the strong El Niño of 2015-2016, California actually had below-average rainfall.

Unprecedented view of cosmos provided by Euclid mission throws up many more cases of gravitational lensing
A mission to create the largest ever 3D map of the universe has revealed more than 900m galaxies in its first major data release together with about 15,000 potential cases of a phenomenon that could help unlock the secrets of the “dark universe”.
Launched in July 2023, the European Space Agency’s Euclid mission promised to create the largest cosmic map ever made, encompassing a third of the sky and more than 10bn years of cosmic history.
The goal is to shed light on two of the biggest mysteries in the universe: the nature of dark energy and dark matter. These are thought to make up about 70% and 25% of the universe respectively.
Prof Andy Taylor, of the University of Edinburgh, who leads the UK science ground segment for the mission, said while there were bigger surveys, none had the detail and the information content of Euclid. By contrast the Hubble telescope has produced images of incredible resolution, but does not cover as large an area of the sky.
“The technological leap that’s Euclid is that we can keep that high resolution, but now we can basically map huge volumes of the sky, huge volumes of the universe,” Taylor said.
Now, the first major Euclid data release has landed, offering researchers an unprecedented view of the cosmos. “It’s the biggest high-resolution image of the universe we’ve ever had,” Taylor said.
Covering about 14% of the total area of sky that will be mapped by Euclid, the newly released data captures over 900m galaxies as well more than 60m potential quasars: blazing objects at the centre of distant galaxies, powered by supermassive black holes.

From the first day of his life, little infant Adnan has suffered a seizure roughly every 13 minutes.
One can only imagine the reactions from his Dubai hospital bedside when, having received a still-experimental drug, his seizures stopped for the day.
And for the week, and the week after that—and the week after that.
The story comes via the Khaleej Times , which reported that the Dubai Health Authority (DHA) granted an application from King’s College Hospital London in Dubai through a “compassionate use” pathway for the use of a drug that is otherwise not approved for commercial use.
Called ABS-1230, the experimental oral medication targets abnormal activity in an ion channel associated with the “extremely rare” form of genetic epilepsy Adnan suffers from.
According to data from the treatment’s developer, Adnan is the youngest patient in the world to receive ABS-1230 and only the second infant to be given the experimental medication.
At the Dubai hospital, sequencing of Adnan’s entire genome revealed a gene variant associated with the seizures and allowed the medical team to identify ABS-1230 as a potential treatment option.
Led by Professor Ubaid Shah, consultant pediatric neurologist and epileptologist at the hospital, the drug was administered on September 14th. The success was so profound and immediate that Adnan was discharged from the hospital with his family just a week later, without a single seizure having been recorded during that time.
“This is an exceptional moment for us, and it highlights what precision medicine can achieve when we are able to identify the genetic cause of a disease and choose a treatment that targets the mechanism linked to it,” Professor Shah told the Times.
Adnan suffered no clinical seizures at his October 11th follow-up. The hospital said he continues to be seizure-free as of November 2nd, and the infant is finally beginning to pass some early development milestones.
“Despite the encouraging response, we will continue to monitor his condition closely to assess whether the results are sustained and whether the experimental treatment is safe,” Professor Shah said.
Indeed, Shah and his colleagues stressed that the treatment is still experimental and requires more research before it can be approved for use by the public. That being said, however, Adnan’s response to it couldn’t have been more positive.

Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call, and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.
The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.

A UFO has landed in Idyllwild, California. Well, sort of. The Donaldson Futuro is a house shaped like an unidentified flying object, sitting on a rock in the southern part of the state. While it can’t zip away, you could be the next owner of this incredible architectural marvel. It’s been put up for sale through Tim McTavish with Sotheby’s International Realty for $1.495 million (at the time of writing).
The unconventional home gets its namesake from owner and former Obama administration appointee Milford Wayne Donaldson and his wife, Laurie Donaldson. The house is listed on the National Register of Historic Places and is architecturally significant. Finnish architect Matti Suuronen designed the prefabricated dwelling in 1969 as a structure that could be transported by helicopter and installed in remote locations. It was intended to adapt to different landscapes, with modular components that are bolted together on site. Four concrete piers support the structure, so it doesn’t require a foundation or conventional construction.
Donaldson Futuro’s aesthetic is a snapshot of design. Suuronen conceived it when designers were fascinated by space exploration (its timing coincides with the moon landing) and advances in synthetic materials. His UFO house reflects tech optimism, imagining a future like the cartoon The Jetsons .
Nearly 60 years later, the 793-square-foot Donaldson Futuro retains its original design integrity. Boasting a yellow fiberglass shell halved by circular windows, its aircraft-style entrance leads to a living area with a kitchen, then onto one bedroom and one bathroom. Light surrounds you at every turn, along with touches of mid-20th-century decor like shag carpeting and bright colors on the cabinetry and walls.
With fewer than 100 Futuros built, the Donaldson Futuro is one of the rarest residential structures in the U.S. Learn more on Sotheby’s International Realty’s website .

It arrived at our solar system’s second-largest planet via a gravitational assist trajectory at Jupiter which was replicated with Voyager 2. On November 12th, when the space probe came within 77,000 miles of Saturn’s cloud-tops, the space probe’s cameras detected complex structures in the rings of Saturn, and its remote sensing instruments studied the atmospheres of Saturn and its giant moon Titan. READ what it discovered… (1980)
Voyager 1 found that about 7% of the volume of Saturn’s upper atmosphere is helium (compared with 11% of Jupiter’s atmosphere), while almost all the rest is hydrogen. Since Saturn’s internal helium abundance was expected to be the same as Jupiter’s and the Sun’s, the lower abundance of helium in the upper atmosphere may imply that the heavier helium may be slowly sinking through Saturn’s hydrogen; that might explain the excess heat that Saturn radiates over energy it receives from the Sun.
Winds blow at high speeds on Saturn. Near the equator, the Voyagers measured winds about 500 m/s (1,100 mph). The wind blows mostly in an easterly direction. Voyager measured the rotation of Saturn (the length of a day) at 10 hours, 39 minutes, 24 seconds, and identified polar aurorae, and aurora-like ultraviolet emissions at middle latitudes. These remain a puzzle to this day, since bombardment by electrons and ions, known to cause auroras on Earth, occurs only at the high latitudes.

About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma?
B rett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout.
“I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?”
Gout has been with us for as long as we know: in 1910 a case was diagnosed in a mummy found near a temple in Upper Egypt. It is the most common form of inflammatory arthritis – and, it is often said, the only curable one – resulting from raised levels of uric acid in the blood. Uric acid is produced when your metabolism breaks down molecules called purines, which are found in your body’s own cells and in certain foods you eat. Excess uric acid is normally processed by the kidneys and passed through urine, but persistently high urate levels can eventually lead to sharp crystals forming in the joints. The presence of these crystals can in turn trigger a profound immune response: inflammation, redness and pain. Eventually, hardened lumps of urate crystals called tophi can form under the skin.
High urate levels can have many causes, but they are not, in themselves, the sole cause of gout. “Virtually all people with gout will have a raised urate level,” says consultant rheumatologist Prof Edward Roddy. “But most people with a raised urate level don’t get gout.”
The pain of a gout attack is so debilitating that it can be hard to describe: the 19th-century writer and clergyman Sydney Smith said it felt “like walking on my eyeballs”. “Sometimes people think they’ve broken a bone – that’s quite a common thing,” says Roddy. “There is some qualitative research showing that people compare the intensity of the pain to having a heart attack or a kidney stone, and that women with gout compare the intensity of the pain to childbirth.”
It can also arrive, in the first instance, with little or no warning. “Often it comes on overnight,” says Roddy. “So somebody goes to bed pain-free, then they wake up and can’t put their foot to the floor.”

items.title: How to spot November's planetary parade in the pre-dawn sky
items.desc: The planets of Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will align in pre-dawn sky throughout November.
items.text:
Stargazers are being treated to a diagonal parade of four planets in the pre-dawn sky throughout November.
Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be visible to the naked eye in the south-eastern to eastern sky.
Particularly notable will be the line-up on Monday 16 November when Mars and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich.
From 24 November, a full Moon - the first of a run of four supermoons - will also join the planets in the morning sky.
Mercury will be the hardest planet to spot in the parade.
As the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in our solar system, it is permanently locked in solar glare.
It is only visible in twilight and never in a fully dark sky. As always it will be dim and close to the horizon.
Try spotting it in a wide open sky with a flat horizon and look to the south-east.
Venus shines in the night sky above a waxing crescent Moon
Above Mercury and toward the right, you will spot Venus.
Venus is an easy planet to find as it is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon. It has the highest albedo of any major planet in our solar system - that is reflects more sunlight back into space thus appearing brighter.
It is also usually the closest planet to Earth in its orbit - a mere 24 million miles away at times. It is a similar size too.
It will be higher in the sky than Mercury and visible earlier in the night in the hours before sunrise.
Don't mistake it with the bright star Spica which will be close to it. Stars twinkle while planets glow steadily.
Mars and Jupiter will appear to be very close to each other in the sky on the 15 and 16 November.
Mars is currently high in the eastern sky, with Jupiter below but appearing brighter.
"They will be separated by just 1.2 degrees, or roughly the width of a finger held at arm's length," according to Gideon Bendavid-Walker, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.
The two planets will appear close to the bright star Regulus and may even look like a triple star.
If you have binoculars or a telescope then a few other bonus planets will also be visible this month.
At a similar time before sunrise, Uranus will be setting in the west. Then Saturn and Neptune will also be visible for a time in the evening rather than the morning sky.

A man put his life on the line to rescue his vulnerable neighbors during a flood in Florida he he described as “biblical.”
With one recovering from surgery and the other stricken with ALS, their survival hinged on help, which their neighbor Rick Addante heroically provided.
It comes amid a flood of stories of compassion and heroism from Brevard County that’s rising as fast as the waters did.
Just yesterday, GNN reported on a woman who was rescued from floodwaters along with her son and 3 dogs by other brave and compassionate neighbors.
Both she and Addante live in Palm Bay, one of several east Florida towns in the path of a 1,000-year rain event that dropped between 16 and 22 inches of rain on Monday alone.
“It was really like a Biblical flood. It just came on so fast and rose so quickly that it caught everyone unprepared,” Addante said.
Addante was particularly concerned for his two vulnerable neighbors across the street. Terry was 80 and had recently undergone open heart surgery, while the other was bound to a motorized wheelchair from amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).
With water up to his knees within the 4 walls of his own house, Terry had spoken to Addante over the phone and said the effort of merely moving about was too much: he could hardly breathe from the strain.
“It was up to his knees inside the house but in the street where we were crossing it was probably up to my shoulders,” Addante told Fox Weather . “I was worried [Terry] was going to get stuck or drown. At first I thought I’d bring him back across the river [street] but it was way too strong.”
Instead, Addante got him out of the house and onto the highest point of his front lawn. He and everyone in the area knew that airboats, like the kind used to navigate the Everglades, were in the neighborhood rescuing people—”they sound like a rocket ship going off.”
Video shared by Addante shows him helping carry out Terry and his dog, Bella, who was terrified of the airboat sounds, with help from Florida Fish and Wildlife officers who were operating the airboats.

A telescope tasked with creating the largest-ever 3D map of the universe is making good on its promise.
On Thursday (Nov. 12), the European Space Agency (ESA) shared the first major data release from its Euclid space telescope , including observations of more than 900 million galaxies and 60 million black-hole-powered light sources in the early universe.
"These are far more than beautiful pictures; today marks a scientific milestone in our study of the cosmos," Carole Mundell , ESA's director of science, said in a statement . "This major Euclid data release represents the largest space-based survey of its kind, laying the foundation of future discovery."
Captured over 13 months, this cornucopia of data covers a slice of sky about 9,500 bigger than the full moon — about 14% of the total sky area that Euclid will survey on its planned six-year mission. Each object in the survey is like a "puzzle piece," with its specific light signature, or spectrum), offering clues about its composition and distance from Earth, according to ESA.
Scientists can now start using the 1.7 million gigabytes of Euclid data to slot those objects into a 3D model of the universe and begin to map out the vast cosmic web that underlies all galaxies. But the data release also includes some stunning space images, which you can enjoy immediately. Here are some of the highlights.
A mosaic of 9 gravitational lenses spotted by the Euclid telescope.
Gravitational lenses are nature's biggest magnifying glasses. These " Einstein rings " ‪—‬ named after Albert Einstein , who predicted their existence — occur when exceptionally massive objects, like large galaxies, bend the fabric of space-time. This cosmic curvature causes the light emitted by objects behind them to appear magnified, distorted and sometimes duplicated.
In its first data release, Euclid has discovered more than 15,000 strong gravitational lensing candidates. These cosmic lenses enable astronomers to get much clearer views of the deep universe than any telescope could possibly see on its own.

Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems
The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems , published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.
Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.
Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.
“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”
Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.
In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

Although booster exploded, company caught upper stage for first time in campaign to make megarocket reusable
SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone in the company’s efforts to make the craft suitable for human spaceflight.
The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22hr mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times.
Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the ocean as with some previous test flights.
The hulking spacecraft is composed of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship.
Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico.
The guidance, navigation and control (GNC) system triggered the no-go.
“It was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, it detected that the booster was not in the place it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said early on Saturday. The booster was also “slightly low on fuel”, according to SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk.
This week’s test flight was still a victory for SpaceX , marking the first time that the company caught its upper stage.
It was also only the second time Starship has entered Earth’s orbit.
The feat comes as the 2028 date nears for Nasa’s plan to return humans to the lunar surface. The agency has contracted SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin for the mission.
“Making more believers by the day,” wrote Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman on X, praising the 15th flight. “One step closer to [the moon].” Isaacman is an ally of Musk, who advised Donald Trump to appoint him to lead Nasa.
SpaceX has plans to ramp up its Starship test flights to a weekly, then twice-weekly cadence, Musk said on a recent earnings call. He has sought to make Starship rapidly reusable so that it can land and take off much like standard airplanes. Musk has touted the rocket’s reusability as a way to reel in the enormous costs of space travel.
Beyond another Moon landing, Musk has also pushed a plan of carrying humans to Mars.

items.desc: School children gather to discuss climate issues to coincide with the COP31 conference in Turkey.
items.text:
Dorset was hit by widespread flooding earlier this year
School children are taking part in an event aimed at inspiring climate action, to coincide with the COP31 international climate conference in Turkey.
Hosted at the Kingston Maurwood campus, the first Dorset-wide Youth COP has brought children from 14 schools together to discuss issues including future careers.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said young people should be "given a voice" over dealing with climate change.
A Dorset COP 2026 event is also being held on Saturday as world leaders and delegates gather at Antalya in Turkey for the COP31 climate summit.
The Dorset Youth COP event includes discussions about how young people feel about climate change as well as a panel session introducing them to the range of jobs and careers in the climate and energy sectors.
Maria Clarke, of Dorset Local Nature Partnership, said: "Young people are inheriting the climate and ecological emergencies that previous generations have created and need to be given a voice in jointly developing and implementing the solutions to these issues."
"The Youth COP aims to raise awareness, inspire and support them to take action now and into the future."
The main Dorset COP 2026 event takes place on Saturday also at the Kingston Maurward Campus near Dorchester.
The fourth annual event brings together community groups, environmental organisations, experts and political leaders.
The programme will explore how Dorset can respond to climate change, nature loss, food resilience, pollution and other environmental challenges.
The programme will also feature an exhibition of over 30 local organisations and a Question Time-style panel bringing together Dorset MPs, council leaders and independent climate experts.
Giles Watts, chair of Dorset CAN said the event's focus was on making "a lasting positive impact" on climate and nature local areas.
"We want to bring people together, listen to different perspectives and energise local communities and politicians to act more quickly on the pressing challenges we face," he added.

An 81-year-old Englishman grew up wondering who his real father was. What he didn’t know was that an entire family tree in Canada was wondering who and where he was.
After being divided by a world war, an ocean, and 8 decades, Rodney Anderson has finally found his long lost relatives with the help of a simple DNA test, and a persistent, curious niece.
“I thought ‘This is a wind up.’ It has to be,” Anderson said, sharing with CBC News the moment he learned of his true origins.
“But it wasn’t. You can’t believe what a shock it is to get that knowledge.”
Anderson’s mother had a child with a visiting Canadian soldier during the Second World War, a secret that his mother and grandmother never shared with him.
He grew up with no knowledge or explanation of his father’s origins whatsoever because of the stigma attached at the time to these out-of-wedlock births, even though they came about during a period of immense crisis and uncertainty about the future.
Canadian Bethany Allen began searching in 2008 for this mystery uncle of hers after discovering in divorce papers that her grandfather, Charles Blakney, had had a child with a woman in the UK in 1944.
He had first sailed off to war in 1942, leaving behind a wife and daughter in New Brunswick. Blakney served as a motor and driver mechanic with the New Brunswick Rangers and returned home in 1945, the same year that Rodney Anderson was born in Farnham to his mother Yvonne. Rumors of his affair overseas remained in the family long after the guns fell silent in Europe.
“My mother [Rodney’s half-sister] had always wanted to know that [Anderson] had a good life and was happy,” Bethany Allen told CBC News.
It took a long time to confirm the link between the Blakney family in Canada and Anderson in Surrey. It came about through a commercial DNA test from Ancestry.

items.text:
In 1994, David vacationed on the Greek island of Kos with his family for a memorable week in which the English teen met a new pen pal.
There were 12 kids, all from different families, that became a friendly pack. One of them was Jodie, who was 15 at the time.
“You know how kids hang out on holiday, we were all just around the pool table and we decided to swap addresses and be pen pals.”
“Me and Jodie were the only ones that stayed in contact—and we carried on writing to each other for years. A letter every month or so, catching up.”
But after three years of communication, David moved, and the pair lost contact.
Little did they know that 29 years later they would get married.
David McArdle from Newcastle was two years older than Jodie, and they both went on their separate life paths.
It wasn’t until twenty years later that David saw a text message arrive on his mother’s phone from Jodie, saying ‘Happy birthday from me and the girls’.
“I couldn’t believe I found her again,” David told Talk to the Press. “I said to my mum, ‘I didn’t know you had Jodie’s number.’”
He replied to the text immediately (saying it was David) and, after a nail-biting 15-minute wait, Jodie, a teaching assistant, messaged back.
“She said she was so glad to hear from me.
“It turns out, that 15-minute wait for her reply was because she was sobbing her heart out looking at the text. She’d wanted to get in touch, but she thought I was in a relationship so she didn’t want to ruffle any feathers.”
From then on, the two never stop talking on the phone for two years, before eventually meeting in person, for the first time in 24 years, when David drove 300 miles to Cardiff to visit Jodie.
“We sat on the sofa and talked for 12 hours,” recalled David who visited her again two weeks later.
After three years of dating, David proposed at the top of the London Eye Ferris wheel and the pair were soon married.
Now the couple live together in Cardiff but visit Kos, the island they met on, every year in August, back to the apartments where they met and swapped addresses.

A woman has had her faith in humanity restored after neighbors arrived on paddleboards to rescue her and her son during recent flooding in Florida.
Emergency services were unable to reach her, the 911 operator said, as Brittany Grant and her son sat on their kitchen counter while floodwaters rose higher and higher above their floor.
Brevard County was recently hit by what weather reports say is a 1,000 year rain event, which flooded towns like Melbourne, Port Lucie, and Palm Bay where Grant lives with her son and 3 dogs.
Having had no luck with 911, Grant turned to Facebook asking for help. Seeing the social media SOS, neighbor Stephanie Fanguy marshalled her strapping teenage sons Jonah, 15, and Lucas, 17, who immediately planned a navigational rescue.
Embarking on an inflatable paddleboard and a borrowed kayak, Jonah and Lucas reached Grant’s house and got to work getting her son Nikoa out through what appeared on social media to be the kitchen window.
Lucas tried to calm Nikoa, who told Click Orlando he struggles with anxiety, by asking him simple questions and remarking humorously at the weather.
Eventually, mother, son, and their 3 dogs—including one which took up half the paddleboard—were all brought to safety.
“The community came together and saved us,” she said . “If it wasn’t for them, I don’t know how we would have gotten out.”
“My faith in humanity has been restored,” she added, saying that other neighbors had volunteered to help as well.
Lucas and Jonah, meanwhile, had a hero’s mentality: someone needed help and they didn’t think twice.
“Because they needed help and they were in trouble and danger, so just didn’t think about it and just went to help them,” Jonah said.

A lot of people just don’t like going to hospitals because it reminds them of sickness, being ill, or even having to deal with the loss of a loved one. That’s why research on the patient experience has found that folks often feel more stressed and worried when they have to go to a medical center.
Some individuals also experience worse health during hospitalization, which could be because of stress and anxiety, or due to changes in sleep, nutrition, and their illness. That’s why folks are often encouraged to get appropriate rest after returning home from medical treatment, so they can recover physically and emotionally.
There are so many things about hospitals that people don’t know, and professionals say one interesting thing is their upside-down designs, which help make medical centers more resilient. After storms like Hurricane Katrina, healthcare designers figured out ways hospitals can continue working without being affected by emergencies

70 years ago today, the US Supreme Court struck down Alabama’s policy of racial segregation on public buses, ending the Montgomery Bus Boycott , made famous by Rosa Parks. READ more… (1956)
Civil rights lawyers filed a lawsuit in June and a three-judge panel of the District Court ruled 2-1 that “the enforced segregation of black and white passengers on motor buses operating in the City of Montgomery violates the Constitution and laws of the United States” because the conditions deprived people of equal protection under the Fourteenth Amendment.
Alabama and the city appealed, but the decision was summarily affirmed by the Supreme Court, which ordered them to desegregate its buses with an official written notice by federal marshals.
86 years ago today, the animated film Fantasia , conceived and produced by Walt Disney himself, was released. It was only Disney’s third animated film and, though it featured Mickey Mouse in the role of ‘The Sorcerer’s Apprentice’, it had almost no dialogue and consisted of eight pieces of classical music conducted by Leopold Stokowski, including The Nutcracker Suite and Pastoral Symphony .
The 2-hour movie was unable to make a profit that decade, but it was destined to become a classic—and also the 24th-highest-grossing film of all time in the US (adjusted for inflation).
Up until Fantasia’s release, movie soundtracks, LPs, and recordings of all types were presented in mono. Thanks to Disney and Leopold Stokowski’s experimental spirit, the engineering prowess of Bell Labs and RCA—at great cost to Disney— Fantasia brought stereo sound to the masses via a multi-channel system that produced an aural marvel for audiences inside 13 theaters across the country. (1940)
99 years ago today, the Holland Tunnel opened connecting New York and New Jersey under the Hudson River. Consisting of two tubes and made a series of cast iron and steel rings bound with 19 inches of concrete running over 8,000 feet in length, it was designed by Clifford Milburn Holland, the project’s chief engineer, who died in October 1924, before it was completed. It is both a National Historic Landmark and a National Historic Civil and Mechanical Engineering Landmark.
The first tunnel under the Hudson was made in 1910 and was actually for railway lines, while the cars passed over on ferries. items.text:
A 103-year-old D-Day veteran was reunited with his war medals just in time for Remembrance Day.
The story came about through a remarkable coincidence when an amateur WWII historian came across the man’s military record and medals, and contacted the family wondering if he still had them.
“They may be just a piece of metal but the medals are something that I hold very close to my heart,” said veteran Douglas Halley, proudly wearing them on his sweater. “They remind me of all my brothers in arms who I was with who helped me get through in the war.”
Halley was just 20 when he landed on the Normandy beaches with the Royal Artillery in the second wave of troops, having been conscripted into the war out of the shop where he was training to be a butcher.
Born in England’s South Yorkshire, Halley was awarded 3 medals: the 1939-45 Star, the France and Germany Star, and the War Medal 1939-45.
He accidentally left them pinned to his uniform, which he returned at the end of the war in 1945—thus losing them exactly when they were the most prestigious of honors.
Last January, 27-year-old Joseph Smith contacted Halley’s grandson, Luke Halley, after seeing Luke’s Veterans Day (called Remembrance Day in the UK) Facebook post about his grandfather.
Smith has been travelling across the UK documenting veterans’ stories for a project titled, The Last of The Greats . He hopes to document as many veterans’ stories for the younger generation so they can learn about and remember their sacrifices.
SIMILAR STORIES TO THIS: Young Man Interviews 3,000 World War II Vets Over 10-year Project–Preserving Their Stories
It was for this project that Smith came across Halley and his medals, contacted Luke via Facebook, and asked if the veteran still had them. Learning about the accident with the uniform in 1945, Smith helped the Halley family contact the Ministry of Defense and fill out the necessary forms to have the medals returned.
“If I can help a veteran or their family in any way, be it getting hold of medals or finding out further information, it is the least I can do,” Smith told the Southwest News Service. “It is an honor, really.”
